claims.claim: The Silk Roads were a network of overland routes linking China with Central Asia, South Asia, the Middle East, and the Mediterranean; by the first century BCE China was the eastern end and Rome the western end.
The term 'Silk Road' ('Seidenstrasse') was coined by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877 CE, long after the routes were in use.

Along the Silk Roads moved goods such as silk and spices, technologies such as papermaking and gunpowder, religions such as Buddhism and Islam, and diseases including the bubonic plague implicated in the mid-14th-century Black Death.

Temujin was proclaimed Chinggis (Genghis) Khan at a kurultai in 1206; the Mongol Empire became the largest contiguous land empire in history, and under Ogedei the Pax Mongolica united much of Eurasia through the exchange of goods and long-distance travel, with relay stations (yam) serving merchants and diplomats.
The relative safety of Eurasian travel under the Pax Mongolica enabled long-distance journeys such as Marco Polo's (1271-1295) to the Yuan court of Kublai Khan (r. 1260-1294).

The Tang (618-907) and Song (960-1279) dynasties are considered a golden age of Chinese invention, including the discovery of gunpowder (Tang) and movable-type printing (Song); the Ming (1368-1644) followed after the Mongol Yuan was expelled.

The Ming treasure voyages, led by Admiral Zheng He, comprised seven expeditions between 1405 and 1433 under the Yongle Emperor (and the last under his successor), reaching Southeast Asia, India, Arabia, and East Africa.

Historians group the Ottoman (c. 1299-1922), Safavid (1501-1736, Iran), and Mughal (1526-1857, India) empires as 'gunpowder empires,' a term coined by Marshall Hodgson and William McNeill in 1974 that is now widely disputed.
The Ottomans used artillery to take Constantinople in 1453, and Akbar (r. 1556-1605) transformed the Mughal Empire into a centralized state covering most of India.
The Taj Mahal was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan (r. 1628-1658) as a mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal (d. 1631), begun in the early 1630s.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Exact dating of the Taj Mahal's construction
positions: World History Encyclopedia states it was 'Built in 1634 CE'
Other standard accounts date construction from c. 1632 with the full complex completed c. 1653
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson gives the approximate span (begun in the early 1630s, c. 1632) rather than a single precise year, and anchors it to Shah Jahan's reign (1628-1658) and Mumtaz Mahal's death (1631), which all sources agree on.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether gunpowder technology explains the rise of the three empires
positions: Hodgson and McNeill (1974) argued the adoption of gunpowder led to their rise
OpenStax notes this theory is 'largely disputed' today
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents 'gunpowder empires' as a conventional label whose underlying causal theory is now contested, rather than asserting gunpowder as the cause.
